You will likely want to accommodate MCTP endpoints that are on non-default MCTP networks, so I would suggest adding a `MCTPNetworkId` property.

> I don't see MCTPNetworkId being passed to ncsi_cmd (with -m option) in Tested Section in https://gerrit.openbmc.org/c/openbmc/phosphor-networkd/+/74759. Do you think it should include that?

Not really, the Tested: section isn't intended to document every behaviour.

> Also, is MCTPNetworkId property same as InterfaceIndex or is it something different, wondering if we can use the InterfaceIndex property itself?

No, this is separate.

The network ID is provided as part of the `--mctp` argument, for which the usage output states:

```
    --mctp [NET,]EID, -m   Specify MCTP network device.
```

The `NET` component of that is optional, but can be used for specifying a non-default MCTP network ID.

At this stage, I would suggest not combining the net and EID in your schema; the <net>,<eid> format is more intended for command-line utilities.

In your example, you have a bit of awkwardness around the NaN / "None" fields for the unused interface type (ie, `InterfaceIndex` when using MCTP, and `MCTPEndpointId` when using RBT).

Is there a better way to specify when those properties are required or not, rather than always required (and then filled with dummy values)?

We plan to use Phosphor-dbus-interface auto generated bindings, thats why i am marking the properties as all required to avoid too much of try catch handling for missing properties. But in this case, we have NCSITransportType which can help to figure out which are required for which type of interface, so probably i can define "InterfaceIndex", "MCTPEndpointId" as optional. Will try to make some change to accommodate this in next revision of patch.

I think we can use "InterfaceIndex": null instead of NaN, since JSON doesn't support NaN as a valid number. Another advantage of using "InterfaceIndex": null for MCTP is that the xyz.openbmc_project.Configuration.NIC interface would hide this property.

[This might be an opportunity to make things a little more reliable; I am happy to defer this discussion if you don't think it is relevant for this particular change though.]

What would you think about using an actual interface name (rather than index) here?

The interface indexes are certainly not intended to be persistent - it's just defined by the probe order of network devices. A network device that is removed and re-added will have a different index after the re-add. The interfaces names are not *necessarily* persistent either, but they are probably more reliable than the index, and we can enforce persistency to names if required.

The tooling does currently take an index, but we could definitely add functionality to deal with names instead.

Or, alternatively: if we start with an index in this schema, would it be possible to later convert to names?

@jk@ozlabs.org How can we enforce persistency to names? I suppose the names would be getting selected based on some linux config.

> How can we enforce persistency to names? I suppose the names would be getting selected based on some linux config.

Yes, this is typically implemented either by specific driver naming rules (eg, the MCTP-over-i2c interfaces will be assigned a network name that corresponds to the underlying i2c controller device, and those may be persistent), or by a udev rule that applies a persistent name based on some property of the underlying device (say, by bus topology)

... that's not something you would need to cover in this changeset, of course 😊
Using the RBT transports though, you'll probably have persistent names there anyway, as the probe order is generally defined by the platform definition.
Sure, changed to InterfaceName instead of InterfaceId for RBT.

"NIC" is not a type in the way Em specifies configuration.

This would be something like MctpNcsiEndpoint ?  Describing the interface itself, not the fact that it's a "NIC" which could take many forms and have many interfaces on it.
See above, this gets rolled into "type" and can be removed.

Devices do not have an intrinsic "endpoint id".  I understand lots of people want an endpoint Id, but as written this immediately breaks if you put more than one nic in a system, or share a nic across two systems.  We need a "platform" level config file type (that honestly could have the same schema) if we want to do static IPMI/MCTP assignments.
